title: Persistence in War like an Unyielding Buffalo
paragraphs: The spectacle of the tumpai puram situation of a king taking on the enemy king of undaunted prowess and determination and putting him to rout is one of the finest examples of ancient Tamiḻs’ valour capable of moving even the stony hearts. In the battle arena, where the two kings cross swords, the enemy soldiers, afraid of going near a fighter, aim spears and bows at him from a safe distance. The warrior, carrying a sword and a shield, fights with all his might. His sword chops off many a number of enemies, but gets blunted after brushing against a stone. His shield also develops chinks and he offers his body as a shield to take on the innumerable spears and arrows shot at him. Alas! In the end, a sword shining like lightning powers its way towards him and in the same lightning speed rips apart his head from the body. But the severed parts of his
body do not fall on the ground immediately; instead, his head, body, legs and hands keep moving and quivering.
> It is in particular > The theme of undoing the might of an invading monarch > Burning with an overweening pride in his prowess. > > (Poruḷatikāram : Puṟattiṇai iyal, verse 15)

> The life of the warrior in action departing, > With his body having been pierced thick and fast > By the rain of arrows and spears of foemen, > There is the wondrous spectacle of the man in two pieces - > The body standing erect without falling on the ground > In the manner of the leech cut into parts staying alive. > > (Poruḷatikāram : Puṟattiṇai iyal, verse 16)

Men on foot, elephants and cavalry march on to the field, sending shivers down the spine of the enemy. The drums are played on both the sides to herald the start of the war. One of them sounds like the thunder of the summer season, while the other sounds like the storm, crossing through the sea, causing a great upheaval.

The swords blaze through the warfield; the spears are launched from the mighty hands. The arrows, ripping through the air, pierce the stomach of a few lethargic men, announcing that a timid person has no place in the field of war. A few exceptional instances surface in which cowards, whose bodies shiver like strings of a musical instrument, running through in fear are identified and sidelined.

A soldier fighting at a distance witnesses his king, dear to him like his own life, hemmed in by enemy soldiers and commanders like columns of fish. “What, is my king in danger?” he reacts with blood-shot eyes and with hands clutching on to his weapon, he pounces there, much like an injured tiger or rather like a stamped snake.

On both the sides, soldiers form protective rings around their kings and safeguard them. The army commander moves around the columns of his army. In the event of any unexpected setback, he remains unfazed quite like a buffalo, only to single-handedly take on the might of the formidable army of the foe. The buffalo can bear anything. It is given such an honour in puṟam literature.
The enemy king is seen fighting a surging elephant and ultimately getting
killed by being trampled by it.
In the end, when both the kings perish in the war, one of the soldiers rises up in rage on seeing the death of his king. He wrecks vengeance upon the enemy rank by killing a number of soldiers.

In a precarious condition, wherein it could not be categorically established as to who finally won, this verse stands out eulogizing an individual soldier who beheads innumerable enemy soldiers to get even for his king’s death. Look at the following Tolkāppiyam verse:

> The theme of tumpai > Ramifies into twelve substrands: > The three columns of infantry, elephantry and cavalry > That strike terror among the foemen; > The deed of mettle by a warrior > That leaves his charge aside > And puts the enemy soldiers to rout > Who come to surround his king > As he keeps daring them with his spear; > The chiefs of the two contending monarchs > Falling to death in personal combat > Besides their prop for their rulers in action; > The daring of an army chief > That comes up braving the odds like a buffalo > To stand at the head of the rear of his army > As it tends to retreat in disarray; > The grit of a warrior in action > Though he stands disarmed of his weapons; > The death of the warriors > That braved the charging elephants; > The clamour of singing and dancing > Of the warriors of the victorious king > Who felled his enemy king to death along with his elephant; > The annihilation of the two contending monarchs > Along with their kindred folk in deed > In their bloody conflict with swords;

> The famed act of a warrior > Who finds his king felled in action > And rises in ire uncontained to fight the foe > And the feat exceptional of the warrior > That sends columns of enemy’s army into disarray > And goes about waving his brilliant winning sword. > > (Poruḷatikāram : Puṟattiṇai iyal, verse 19)
